title: Designed a difficult minimalist puzzle game, but most players can't get past level 15 and believe the game was done by AI but it is definetly not —how do I find the right audience?
author: Public_Year9033
selftext:
​I recently finished designing and playtesting a difficult minimalist puzzle game. During testing, I noticed a major wall: most people didn't even figure out what the game was actually about. They found it too hard and ended up dropping off before or right around level 15 and believed it is done by AI but I really did most the job myself.

​I'm trying to figure out how to find the right audience for this specific niche—people who actually enjoy tough, minimalist puzzles—and how to encourage them to keep going further instead of quitting early on.

​I can't post a link here to avoid getting banned for self-promotion, but if anyone is willing to check it out and give me feedback, let me know and I can send you the link via DM.

comments.author: johnesco
comments.body: DM me, and I'd be happy to playtest it and give some feedback. Or we can chat here.

replies.author: johnesco
replies.body: It's interesting, I'd introduce the tools more gradually giving an explanation (even if it just shows the user the existing instruction page). The naming on the tools is clear in most cases, but because selection order matters, we need a way to see what will affect what. Will keep playing, let me know if you make any updates.

comments.author: 2eggs1stone
comments.body: My suggestion for puzzle games is to have the hardest puzzles available as optional progression.  Have the more basic puzzles be the "core game" and act as a funnel for building your audience while having the more difficult puzzles as a side objective.  Then cater to the hardcore audience that enjoys the more difficult puzzles as the game's user base grows.
